request: Returns are killing us. I need to see what's going on.

questions.question: What decision will this help you make? For example: (a) fix problem products or brands, (b) change a return policy, (c) find which customers or channels send back the most, or (d) something else?
questions.why: Decision the dashboard supports; the premise that returns are a problem is unverified, so the dashboard should show whether and where returns are high.
questions.answer: (a) Fix problem products or brands. I want to see which categories and brands to review with suppliers, so I'm focusing on the ones with enough volume to matter.

questions.question: How should we measure "returns"? Option 1: share of items sold that were returned (returned items ÷ items sold). Option 2: share of orders with at least one returned item. Option 3: the money value of returned items (at retail price). Which one, or a combination?
questions.why: Defines the main KPI; return rate is ambiguous.
questions.answer: Option 1, returned items divided by items delivered or returned, with cancelled items left out. That's the measure I need for picking which categories and brands to take to suppliers.

questions.question: You want to focus on categories and brands with enough volume to matter. What cut-off should count as enough? For example: at least 100 items sold in the period, at least 500, or the top 20 by items sold. If unsure, I can propose one.
questions.why: Defines the volume threshold to avoid noisy small-sample rates.
questions.answer: I don't have a set number. Something like a few hundred items sold over the 12 months seems like enough to be worth a supplier conversation, so go ahead and propose a cutoff.

questions.question: What time period and comparison do you want? Options: (a) last 12 months only, (b) last 12 months vs the 12 months before, (c) monthly trend over the last 24 months with a 12-month total. Data runs to September 2026.
questions.answer: Last 12 months only, October 2025 through September 2026, with a month-by-month trend. I don't need the comparison to the prior year.

questions.question: Who will read this dashboard? For example: just you, the merchandising/buying team, or senior leadership? And do you want to be able to filter by department (e.g. Men/Women) too?
questions.why: Audience and filters; required before submission.
questions.answer: Mostly me, and the merchandising team will probably look at it too. I don't need a department filter; category and brand are enough.

brief.business_question: Which product categories and brands have the highest return rates over the last 12 months (October 2025 to September 2026), among those with enough sales volume to matter, and how has the return rate moved month by month?
brief.audience: The requester (primary) and the merchandising team.
brief.decision_supported: Choose which categories and brands to review with suppliers because of high return rates.

kpis.name: Return rate (items)
kpis.plain_definition: Returned items divided by items that were delivered or returned. Cancelled items are left out of both the top and the bottom. Items still in process or shipped but not yet delivered are also left out. Calculated over October 2025 to September 2026.

kpis.name: Items sold (volume)
kpis.plain_definition: Count of items that were delivered or returned (same base as the return rate denominator), over October 2025 to September 2026. Used to apply the volume cut-off.

kpis.name: Returned items
kpis.plain_definition: Count of items with a return, over October 2025 to September 2026. Shown next to the rate so the size of the problem is clear.

brief.time_range: October 2025 through September 2026 (last 12 months), with a month-by-month trend.
brief.comparison: None. No comparison to the prior year. Overall company return rate shown as a reference line only if approved (see assumptions).
open_assumptions: Volume cut-off: a category or brand needs at least 300 items delivered or returned across the 12 months to be ranked. Those below are hidden from the ranking (or shown as 'low volume'). Please approve or change the number.
Items are assigned to a month by the order date, not the return date. Please confirm.
Items that are still processing or shipped (not yet delivered) are excluded, since their outcome is unknown. This follows from the stated definition.
Monthly trend is shown for the overall rate and for any selected category or brand. Monthly figures for small brands may be noisy.
The company-wide return rate is shown as a benchmark so the reader can see whether a category or brand is above or below average. This was not requested and needs approval.
Return rate is counted in items, not orders or money value, as the stakeholder chose.
out_of_scope: The reasons for returns (e.g. wrong size, defective) cannot be shown unless the data records them. The data described covers orders, items, products and customers, with no return reason.
Supplier-level analysis is not possible as a separate view. The data has brand but no supplier field, so brand is used as the proxy.
Comparison to the prior year was not requested and is not included.

mappings.logic: Grain is order_items. Numerator = count of items with status = 'Returned'. Denominator = count of items with status in ('Complete','Returned'). Cancelled, Shipped and Processing are left out of both. Rate = numerator / denominator, limited to items created in Oct 2025 to Sep 2026.

Count of order_items rows with status in ('Complete','Returned') and created_at in the 12-month window. This is the same as the return rate denominator. It drives the 300-item cut-off, which is applied to the 12-month total for each category or brand.
Count of order_items rows with status = 'Returned' and created_at in the 12-month window. Status is used, not returned_at, so the item is counted in the month it was ordered.
Join order_items to products on product_id = id. Group items by products.category. Compute the KPIs per category. Rank only categories with 300 or more items sold.

Join order_items to products. Group items by products.brand. Compute the KPIs per brand. Rank only brands with 300 or more items sold. Items with a null brand (about 0.1% of products) go in an 'Unknown' group or are excluded. This needs a decision.

Month = calendar month of order_items.created_at (UTC). Compute the return rate per month, for all items and for any selected category or brand. This follows the approved rule to use the order date, not the return date.
Filter order_items, via the join to products, to the chosen category or categories. It applies to the ranking, the KPIs and the trend.
Filter order_items, via the join to products, to the chosen brand or brands. It applies to the ranking, the KPIs and the trend.

mappings.item: Time range: October 2025 through September 2026, monthly trend
mappings.logic: Keep items with created_at >= 2025-10-01 and < 2026-10-01 (UTC). The upper bound matters because order_items has rows dated into early October 2026, and those must be excluded. Bucket by month for the trend.
Same formula as the return rate with no category or brand grouping. Use all items in the window, including those from low-volume categories and brands. Show it as a reference line only if approved.

gaps.reason: No column records why an item was returned. There is only a status and a returned_at date.
There is no supplier field. Brand is the closest field, but a brand may not match a supplier.
gaps.substitute: products.brand as a proxy for supplier

gaps.item: A fully reliable return rate for the most recent months
gaps.reason: Status is the current status only, with no history. Recent orders have had less time to be returned, so their rate is probably understated. Items that are Complete now may still be returned later. This mostly affects the last 1 to 2 months, and the trend may look like it is improving when it is not.
gaps.substitute: Show the trend, but mark the latest months as incomplete. You can also compare against older months only for items of a similar age.

data_notes: Use order_items.status, not orders.status. Items in one order can have different statuses, and the brief counts items.

'Delivered or returned' is taken as status in ('Complete','Returned'). delivered_at is about 65% null, so it may not match status. Check this against status before sign-off. Returned items may not have a delivered_at value.

order_items.created_at and orders.created_at differ slightly (for example, 04:46 vs 05:37 on the first day). Items near a month boundary could land in different months depending on which one is used. This mapping uses order_items.created_at and does not need the orders table.
order_items has rows created up to 2026-10-04, but orders ends at 2026-09-30. Apply the upper bound of < 2026-10-01 so September 2026 is complete and consistent.

The 300-item cut-off will probably leave very few brands. There are 2,756 brands and only about 171k items across all years, so most brands will have well under 300 items in 12 months. Check how many brands pass before the cut-off is approved. A lower cut-off or a top-N view may be needed.
Monthly trend by brand or category will be based on small counts. Monthly cut-offs are not applied, so small groups will look noisy.

Some category names overlap or are near-duplicates: 'Socks' and 'Socks & Hosiery', 'Pants' and 'Pants & Capris', 'Suits' and 'Suits & Sport Coats'. 'Blazers & Jackets' is also close to 'Outerwear & Coats'. Left as they are, they split volume and can push categories under the cut-off. The merchandising team should decide whether to merge them.
Brand is free text, with 2,756 distinct values and about 0.1% null. Spelling variants of one brand would be counted as separate brands.
Revenue is not needed for these KPIs, so sale_price is not used. Return rate is by item count only, as chosen.
The time window is fixed at Oct 2025 to Sep 2026. Use the data's own latest date (30 Sep 2026), not today's date, when you define 'last 12 months'.
users is not needed. Personal fields (first_name, last_name, email) must not appear in the dashboard.

audit.summary: I found no high-risk problems. The brief counts items by status and groups them by order month, category and brand, so most of these issues only touch columns we don't use. The two that can change the ranking are the 5 items with no matching product and the 5 misspelled categories. Both are tiny, and both can be fixed with simple rules.

issues.explanation: Five items point to products that do not exist (IDs 30001 to 30005). We can't tell their category or brand. They would drop out of the category and brand ranking but could still be counted in the company-wide rate. That would make the totals disagree. The effect is tiny.
issues.proposed_rule: Exclude order items whose product_id is not in products.id from every KPI, including the company-wide benchmark, so all views use the same base. Log the excluded count.
issues.rule: every order_items.product_id must exist in products.id

issues.explanation: Five products have a category spelled differently, such as 'JEANS', 'jeans ', 'Sweater', 'Tops and Tees' and 'Accesories'. They are the same categories as the main spellings. Left alone, they would show up as extra tiny categories. They would also be left out of the real category counts. Only 5 products are affected, so the impact is small. It is still wrong in a dimension we rank on.
issues.proposed_rule: Trim spaces and map to the standard names: JEANS and 'jeans ' to Jeans, 'Tops and Tees' to 'Tops & Tees', Sweater to Sweaters, Accesories to Accessories. Apply this before grouping. Also check brand for the same problem.
issues.rule: rare spellings of a common value: 'JEANS' looks like 'Jeans'; 'jeans ' looks like 'Jeans'; 'Tops and Tees' looks like 'Tops & Tees'; 'Sweater' looks like 'Sweaters'; 'Accesories' looks like 'Accessories'

issues.explanation: Five items have a zero or negative sale price, which is not valid for a sale. No KPI in the brief uses price, because return rate is counted in items. These rows do not distort the numbers today. They would distort any money measure if one were added later. They could also be test rows or refund lines.
issues.proposed_rule: Keep these rows for item-count KPIs, since status decides whether an item counts. Exclude order items with sale_price <= 0 from any future money-based measure. Flag them to the data owner.

issues.explanation: 637 returned items have a return time before the order time. The timestamps are wrong. The brief assigns items to months by order date and counts returns by status, so the counts do not change. It does confirm that returned_at should not be used. The month by return date would be unreliable.
issues.proposed_rule: Count a return from the item status, not from returned_at. Assign the month from created_at. Do not calculate any time-to-return measure from these rows.
issues.rule: returned_at must not be before created_at

issues.explanation: 5,761 items show a delivery time before the order time. The timestamps are wrong. The brief does not use delivered_at. It decides delivered items by status and groups by order date. The numbers are safe as long as status is used.
issues.proposed_rule: Use the status field to decide which items are delivered. Do not use delivered_at for filtering or for month assignment. Do not report delivery-time measures from this column.
issues.rule: delivered_at must not be before created_at

issues.explanation: 33,766 items show a shipping time before the order time. This is a large share, so the shipping timestamps cannot be trusted. The brief does not use shipped_at. It only needs status and order date, so the KPIs are not affected.
issues.proposed_rule: Do not use shipped_at in this dashboard. Use status to exclude items that are still processing or shipped. Report the issue to the data owner.
issues.rule: shipped_at must not be before created_at

time_window.explanation: The 12 complete calendar months ending at the last day of data (30 Sep 2026). Items are placed in a month by order_items.created_at (UTC). Use created_at >= 2025-10-01 and < 2026-10-01, because order_items has rows dated into early October 2026 that must be left out.

shared_rules: Base table is order_items joined to products on order_items.product_id = products.id. One row is one item.

Status comes from order_items.status, never from orders.status. 'Sold' means status in ('Complete','Returned'). 'Returned' means status = 'Returned'. Cancelled, Shipped and Processing are left out of both the top and the bottom of every rate.
Month and period come from order_items.created_at (UTC), the order date. Do not use returned_at, delivered_at or shipped_at anywhere. Their timestamps are wrong for many rows.
Exclude order items whose product_id is not in products.id (IDs 30001 to 30005) from every metric, including the company-wide reference. Log how many were excluded.

Clean category before grouping: trim spaces and map 'JEANS' and 'jeans ' to 'Jeans', 'Tops and Tees' to 'Tops & Tees', 'Sweater' to 'Sweaters', 'Accesories' to 'Accessories'. Do not combine any other categories. Overlapping pairs (Socks and Socks & Hosiery, Pants and Pants & Capris, Suits and Suits & Sport Coats) stay separate, as in the data.
Clean brand before grouping: trim spaces and ignore upper/lower case differences. Other spelling variants are not merged, and this is noted as a limit.
Keep items with sale_price <= 0 (5 rows). Status decides if an item counts. No metric here uses price.

Volume cut-off (confirmed): a category or brand is ranked only if its 12-month items sold is at least 300. The same 300 applies to categories and brands. Items from groups below the cut-off stay in the overall totals and the company-wide rate. They are shown as one 'Below cut-off' row, not listed one by one.

Brands: rank the top 15 by return rate among brands that pass the cut-off. If fewer than 15 pass, show only those that pass. Ties go to more returned items, then to name A to Z. Categories: show every category that passes the cut-off.
Items with a null brand are grouped as 'Unknown'. 'Unknown' is not ranked as a brand but stays in category totals and overall totals.
Category and brand filters apply to the ranking tables, the KPIs and the trend. The company-wide reference line ignores the filters.
No personal fields (name, email) appear anywhere.

decisions_confirmed: How many items should a brand or category need before it can be ranked? We expect very few of the 2,756 brands to reach 300 items in 12 months. Answer: 300 for both is fine. That's in line with what I said, and I'd rather see a short list of brands that really matter than a long list of noisy ones.

Some categories overlap: Socks and Socks & Hosiery, Pants and Pants & Capris, Suits and Suits & Sport Coats. Should we combine each pair? Answer: Keep them separate as they are in the data for now. I don't want to guess at groupings before a supplier conversation, and I'll check with merchandising if one of them comes up as a candidate.

check_in.question: How many items should a brand or category need before it can be ranked? We expect very few of the 2,756 brands to reach 300 items in 12 months. Options: 300 items for both categories and brands; 300 for categories, 100 for brands; 300 for categories, and for brands the 50 with the most items sold. I'd suggest: 300 items for both categories and brands, unless you prefer otherwise. (A higher cut-off may leave only a handful of brands on the ranking, and a lower one adds more brands but with noisier rates.)
check_in.answer: 300 for both is fine. That's in line with what I said, and I'd rather see a short list of brands that really matter than a long list of noisy ones.

Options: Keep them separate, as they are in the data; Combine the three obvious pairs; Let merchandising give us the mapping first. sql.sql:
WITH items AS (
  SELECT
    oi.id,
    oi.status,
    CASE UPPER(TRIM(p.category))
      WHEN 'JEANS' THEN 'Jeans'
      WHEN 'TOPS AND TEES' THEN 'Tops & Tees'
      WHEN 'SWEATER' THEN 'Sweaters'
      WHEN 'ACCESORIES' THEN 'Accessories'
      ELSE TRIM(p.category)
    END AS category_clean,
    LOWER(NULLIF(TRIM(p.brand), '')) AS brand_key,
    NULLIF(TRIM(p.brand), '') AS brand_trim
  FROM `analyst-agent-512103.thelook_dirty.order_items` oi
  JOIN `analyst-agent-512103.thelook_dirty.products` p ON oi.product_id = p.id
  WHERE oi.created_at >= TIMESTAMP('2025-10-01')
    AND oi.created_at < TIMESTAMP('2026-10-01')
    AND oi.status IN ('Complete', 'Returned')
),
cat AS (
  SELECT category_clean AS group_name, COUNT(*) AS items_sold, COUNTIF(status = 'Returned') AS items_returned
  FROM items GROUP BY 1
),
cat_ranked AS (
  SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY SAFE_DIVIDE(items_returned, items_sold) DESC, items_returned DESC, group_name ASC) AS rnk
  FROM cat WHERE items_sold >= 300
),
brand AS (
  SELECT brand_key,
         COALESCE(MAX(brand_trim), 'Unknown') AS group_name,
         COUNT(*) AS items_sold,
         COUNTIF(status = 'Returned') AS items_returned
  FROM items GROUP BY brand_key
),
brand_ranked AS (
  SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY SAFE_DIVIDE(items_returned, items_sold) DESC, items_returned DESC, group_name ASC) AS rnk
  FROM brand WHERE items_sold >= 300 AND brand_key IS NOT NULL
),
excluded AS (
  SELECT COUNT(*) AS n_items, COUNTIF(oi.status = 'Returned') AS n_returned
  FROM `analyst-agent-512103.thelook_dirty.order_items` oi
  LEFT JOIN `analyst-agent-512103.thelook_dirty.products` p ON oi.product_id = p.id
  WHERE p.id IS NULL
    AND oi.created_at >= TIMESTAMP('2025-10-01')
    AND oi.created_at < TIMESTAMP('2026-10-01')
    AND oi.status IN ('Complete', 'Returned')
),
result AS (
  SELECT 1 AS table_order, 0 AS row_order, 'Overall (12 months)' AS table_name, 'All items' AS group_name,
         CAST(NULL AS INT64) AS rank_by_return_rate, COUNT(*) AS items_sold, COUNTIF(status = 'Returned') AS items_returned
  FROM items
  UNION ALL
  SELECT 2, 0, 'Category', group_name, rnk, items_sold, items_returned FROM cat_ranked
  UNION ALL
  SELECT 2, 1, 'Category', 'Below cut-off', NULL, SUM(items_sold), SUM(items_returned)
  FROM cat WHERE items_sold < 300 HAVING COUNT(*) > 0
  UNION ALL
  SELECT 3, 0, 'Brand (top 15)', group_name, rnk, items_sold, items_returned FROM brand_ranked WHERE rnk <= 15
  UNION ALL
  SELECT 3, 1, 'Brand (top 15)', 'Below cut-off', NULL, SUM(items_sold), SUM(items_returned)
  FROM brand WHERE items_sold < 300 HAVING COUNT(*) > 0
  UNION ALL
  SELECT 3, 2, 'Brand (top 15)', 'Unknown (not ranked)', NULL, items_sold, items_returned
  FROM brand WHERE brand_key IS NULL AND items_sold >= 300
  UNION ALL
  SELECT 4, 0, 'Excluded: product not in catalog', 'Items left out', NULL, n_items, n_returned FROM excluded
)
SELECT
  table_name,
  group_name,
  rank_by_return_rate,
  items_sold,
  items_returned,
  SAFE_DIVIDE(items_returned, items_sold) AS return_rate
FROM result
ORDER BY table_order, row_order, rank_by_return_rate, group_name

findings: Suits & Sport Coats (31.4%), Socks (30.7%) and Leggings (30.5%) have the highest return rates among categories with at least 300 items, against a company rate of 28.2%.
The category spread is narrow: from Underwear at 23.8% up to Suits & Sport Coats at 31.4%, so no category is far from the average.

Only three brands reach 300 items in 12 months: Carhartt (28.2%), Allegra K (28.1%) and Calvin Klein (26.3%). None is clearly above the company rate, so this data does not point to a brand to raise with suppliers.
The other 2,714 brands sit below the cut-off and are not ranked, so brand-level problems may be hidden by low volume.

The monthly rate moved between 25.2% (July 2026) and 30.8% (November 2025) with no clear upward or downward trend; August and September 2026 are incomplete because returns are still arriving, so those rates are likely understated.

Similar categories are kept separate as agreed: Pants (30.0%) and Pants & Capris (29.0%), Socks (30.7%) and Socks & Hosiery (27.9%). The data does not record return reasons or suppliers, so it cannot explain why items come back.
